outputs.L1: For dynamical dark energy cosmologies, we perform a series of gravitational N-body simulations that achieve percent-level accuracy in the relative matter power spectra at any redshift. This level of precision is essential for next-generation cosmological matter probes. Our matching procedure reproduces the CMB distance to the surface of last scattering and yields subpercent-level accuracy in the power spectra at \(z=0\) and \(z\sim3\). We discuss the physical implications of these results for probing dark energy through large-scale structure surveys.
outputs.L2: We perform a suite of gravitational N-body simulations for cosmological models with evolving dark energy, obtaining percent-level precision in relative mass power spectra across all redshifts. This degree of accuracy is required for upcoming cosmological probes of the matter distribution. Our matching method preserves the CMB distance to the surface of last scattering and achieves subpercent accuracy in the power spectra at both \(z=0\) and \(z\sim3\). We also examine what these results imply for constraining dark energy through large-scale structure surveys.
outputs.L3:
This study presents N-body gravitational simulations designed to investigate cosmological models with dynamical dark energy. The simulations achieve percent-level accuracy in the relative matter power spectrum across all relevant redshifts, meeting the precision requirements of next-generation cosmological probes of the matter distribution.

A central element of the approach is a matching procedure that reproduces the cosmic microwave background distance to the surface of last scattering. By ensuring this key geometric quantity is preserved, the method enables accurate comparisons between dynamical dark energy models and corresponding reference cosmologies. The resulting matter power spectra reach subpercent-level accuracy at both \(z=0\) and \(z\sim3\). This precision makes the simulations particularly valuable for dark energy studies based on large-scale structure surveys, including measurements of galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing.
outputs.L4:
N-body simulations are essential for predicting how dark energy affects the nonlinear growth of cosmic structure. For dynamical dark energy models, however, the equation-of-state parameter \(w(a)\) varies with time, making it computationally expensive to simulate the full range of possible histories. A practical alternative is to associate each dynamical model with an auxiliary constant-\(w\) cosmology whose parameters are chosen through a matching procedure.

The central requirement is that the auxiliary cosmology reproduce the comoving distance from the redshift of interest to the surface of last scattering measured by the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The models are also assigned compatible physical matter and baryon densities, primordial spectra, and fluctuation amplitudes. Because the distance to last scattering depends on the integrated expansion history, this construction captures much of the influence of dynamical dark energy on structure formation while allowing the use of simulations or fitting formulas developed for constant-\(w\) models. A different auxiliary cosmology can be selected at each output redshift, so the procedure follows the evolving dynamical model rather than approximating its entire history with a single effective equation of state.

Comparisons of high-resolution N-body simulations show that matched cosmologies have remarkably similar matter power spectra, including in the nonlinear regime. The relevant quantity is the relative power spectrum—the ratio between the prediction for a dynamical dark energy model and that for an appropriate reference cosmology—because many numerical and modeling uncertainties cancel in this ratio. At \(z=0\), the matched constant-\(w\) model reproduces the dynamical model’s spectrum to substantially better than one percent over the scales tested. Comparable subpercent agreement is also obtained at high redshift, around \(z\simeq3\), indicating that the method remains accurate well beyond the present epoch. At intermediate redshifts, percent-level accuracy can be maintained by applying the matching separately at each epoch.

This result provides an efficient route to predictions for a broad class of evolving dark energy scenarios. Instead of running a dedicated simulation for every possible function \(w(a)\), one can construct a smaller library of constant-\(w\) simulations and map dynamical models onto it using the CMB-distance criterion. The approach reduces the computational burden while retaining the precision required for observables such as weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, and redshift-space distortions.

Such accuracy is important for next-generation large-scale-structure surveys, whose statistical uncertainties will be small enough that theoretical errors at the percent level can bias cosmological constraints. By reproducing relative matter power spectra at subpercent accuracy at both low and high redshift, the matching method offers a practical foundation for testing whether dark energy is consistent with a cosmological constant or evolves over cosmic time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a research paper on high-accuracy N-body simulations of dynamical dark energy cosmologies and their relevance to future large-scale-structure surveys.
counterfactuals.output: We present a suite of high-accuracy N-body simulations for dynamical dark energy cosmologies, spanning time-dependent equations of state and associated variations in cosmic expansion and structure growth. Using stringent force, mass, and time resolution criteria, we quantify the impact of dark energy evolution on the nonlinear matter power spectrum, halo mass function, and halo clustering, while assessing numerical convergence and sensitivity to initial conditions. Dynamical dark energy produces scale- and redshift-dependent signatures that can exceed the precision requirements of upcoming large-scale-structure surveys. The simulations provide benchmarks for perturbative models, fitting functions, and emulators, enabling robust predictions for weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, and cluster abundance. These results highlight the need for percent-level nonlinear modeling to extract unbiased constraints on dark energy from next-generation surveys.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a cosmology study that matches the CMB distance to last scattering and achieves subpercent accuracy in relative matter power spectra at \(z=0\) and \(z\sim3\).
counterfactuals.output:
The study tested **“CMB-distance matching”**—also called **spectral equivalence**—for dynamical dark-energy cosmologies. For each model with a time-dependent equation of state, typically \(w(a)=w_0+w_a(1-a)\), the authors constructed an auxiliary constant-\(w\) cosmology that had:

- the same physical matter and baryon densities, \(\omega_m\) and \(\omega_b\);
- the same primordial spectrum;
- the same linear fluctuation amplitude at the redshift being compared; and
- the same comoving distance from that redshift to the CMB last-scattering surface.

High-resolution \(N\)-body simulations showed that, despite different expansion and growth histories, the **relative nonlinear matter power spectra** of the paired cosmologies agreed at the **subpercent level at \(z=0\)** and remained comparably accurate at **\(z\simeq3\)** over the resolved weakly and strongly nonlinear scales.

The result implies that much of the nonlinear impact of smooth dynamical dark energy is encoded by the physical densities, growth normalization, and integrated distance to recombination. Consequently, constant-\(w\) simulation grids or emulators can be used to predict spectra for a broader class of evolving-\(w\) models by constructing a redshift-dependent matched cosmology. The prescription is less secure for models with substantial early dark energy, modified gravity, clustering dark energy, massive-neutrino differences, or baryonic effects not included in the matching.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short scientific paragraph explaining how gravitational simulations can model the matter power spectrum in evolving dark energy scenarios with percent-level precision.
counterfactuals.output: High-resolution gravitational \(N\)-body simulations can predict the matter power spectrum in evolving dark energy models by incorporating the model-dependent expansion history and linear growth rate into the particle dynamics and initial conditions. Suites of simulations spanning dark energy parameter space can then be used to calibrate fitting functions or train emulators for the nonlinear power spectrum. Achieving percent-level precision requires large simulation volumes, sufficient mass and force resolution, accurate time integration, and careful control of sample variance and numerical systematics. Validation against higher-resolution runs and independent simulation codes ensures robust predictions over the relevant redshift and wavenumber ranges.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an astronomy conference abstract about a matching procedure for dynamical dark energy models, emphasizing N-body simulations, CMB constraints, and implications for next-generation mass probes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Matching Dynamical Dark Energy Cosmologies for Precision N-body Predictions**

We present a matching procedure that maps dynamical dark energy cosmologies onto auxiliary constant-\(w\) models optimized for high-accuracy N-body simulations. At each target redshift, the auxiliary cosmology is chosen to preserve the physical matter and baryon densities, the primordial spectrum, and the comoving distance to the surface of last scattering, while matching the linear growth normalization at that epoch. This construction maintains consistency with primary cosmic microwave background constraints and isolates the late-time effects of the dark energy expansion history.

Using suites of gravity-only N-body simulations spanning representative \(w(a)=w_0+w_a(1-a)\) models, we test the correspondence in the nonlinear matter power spectrum, halo mass function, and halo clustering. The matched constant-\(w\) simulations reproduce the dynamical models substantially more accurately than mappings based only on the instantaneous equation of state or on equal present-day \(\sigma_8\). Residual differences provide a direct measure of sensitivity to the full growth history and identify the scales and redshifts where baryonic modeling, massive neutrinos, or dedicated dynamical-dark-energy simulations become necessary.

This framework enables existing constant-\(w\) simulation libraries and emulators to be extended efficiently across a broad class of time-dependent dark energy models without requiring a new simulation grid for every expansion history. It is therefore well suited to next-generation mass probes—including weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, cluster abundance, and their cross-correlations—whose constraining power depends on percent-level control of nonlinear structure formation while remaining anchored to CMB-calibrated initial conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In 3–4 sentences, describe research using N-body simulations to predict nonlinear mass power spectra across redshift and assess dark energy through large-scale-structure surveys.
counterfactuals.output: Researchers run suites of high-resolution N-body simulations across a grid of cosmological parameters to model the nonlinear evolution of matter and predict the mass power spectrum over a broad redshift range. These simulations are used to build fast emulators or fitting functions that achieve percent-level accuracy beyond the reach of linear perturbation theory. Comparing the predictions with weak-lensing, galaxy-clustering, and related large-scale-structure measurements enables surveys to constrain the dark-energy equation of state and its possible evolution. Careful modeling of baryonic effects, galaxy bias, and observational systematics is essential to avoid biased conclusions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
